title: Is it cheaper/better to use local AI models than run them on rented hardware?
author: PoopsMcScoots
selftext:
I don’t know about you but I’m getting MAJOR subscription fatigue.

Subscription after subscription after subscription.

Then they lead you to an inflated pay-as-you-go model.

At the end of the day you are paying for their cloud hardware at massively marked up rates compared to renting it.

 It just seems like it’s potentially better and cheaper to just rent GPUs and then working while it’s on.

comments.author: IndianaNetworkAdmin
comments.body:
It depends on your electric bill and your total usage.

The 5090 can pull 575W. That's a lot of power for 32GB, but it lets you run smaller models very fast. If you include the rest of your computer on top, that's 800-900W at full load.

Compare that to a Mac Studio M3 (Going for older/slower just for comparison's sake) it pulls 270W max.

The wattage per token generated is about the same, as the 5090 is 2-3x faster but also consumes 2-3x power. So if you're doing this during specific hours of the day, the 5090 is the way to go, and that sets up your comparison point.

But if you want something 24/7 and always on, the Mac uses \~10W when idle versus a 5090+CPU+etc at \~100W (Estimate, there are a lot of configurations).

What I do is I have a couple $20 subscriptions, because different frontier models are good at different things. Then I have a llama-swap setup on my M3 Ultra with DS Flash, GLM 5.3 Flash, all the small Qwen models, etc.

My frontier models are given access to use my local for agentic work. This means I don't have to get the $200/month to get things done. I often have jobs that run overnight, which is why the Mac made more sense than an NVidia machine.

I don't hit 5-hour quota limits, and at the end of every week I usually have usage to burn on anything that's giving the local models trouble. Frontier orchestrates, local builds.

Edit: It sounded like you were comparing renting versus running local against your current subscriptions, so I answered from that perspective. Either way, you would evaluate the cost of a local system against the cost of renting GPUs, so you need to know which local option is best for you in order to weigh against renting.

comments.author: RemarkableWish2508
comments.body:
> you are paying for their cloud hardware at massively marked up rates

That's not all the story behind cloud services.

Markup rates are relative to 100% hardware utilization, since cloud services can get a different user when you're done. Can you do the same? If you rent some hardware, and let it lie idle, you're effectively paying a markup on the time you are actively using it.

Datacenters have economies of scale for specific hardware, power, bandwidth, cooling, maintenance, and support. You can get some of that by renting a bare metal server, you won't get much of it at home.

In the case of AI, the minimum hardware required to run frontier models, has a hefty price tag... and the real frontier models are privative, not even OpenWeights.

While it is wise to compare cloud costs against an on-prem setup, be sure to include all costs, and compare apples to apples, not to oranges.

comments.author: arelath
comments.body:
I've looked into this quite a bit and do rent gpus for any training I can't do locally. For inferance though, it's almost always cheaper to pay the per token rates on a service like openrouter. This is because you can batch multiple requests together basically for free since LLMs are memory bandwidth limited, not computational limited. It really depends on the hardware you're running on, but typically 4 requests can be batched together for 4x the throughput on the same hardware. 

So unless you're running at least 4 agents at a time, you're not using the full capacity of the hardware. And because agents aren't streaming requests 100% of the time, you'd really need to be running more like 16 agents at a time to really utilize the full gpu potential.

Assuming you aren't running loads like this, the cloud providers can sell the extra capacity when you are paying per token. So renting gpus for inferance almost always ends up being more expensive.

Sometimes you can make the numbers work if you get a really good rate on rented GPU time. For instance, this week I've been renting 3090s for $0.22/hour. This is so insanely cheap, especially when you can rent machines with 2x-4x 3090s, that you could make it work.

I have been very tempted to run open models on renter gpus just to get fast token rates though.
